name: Cortagen
lead: Cortagen is a synthetic tetrapeptide with the sequence Ala-Glu-Asp-Pro, made by Vladimir Khavinson's group in Russia from the amino-acid analysis of Cortexin, a natural brain-cortex peptide preparation [1]. It is one of the short synthetic peptide bioregulators the group proposes as tissue-specific regulators of ageing-related changes, alongside Epithalon (Ala-Glu-Asp-Gly) and Vilon (Lys-Glu) [1][3].

In longevity and biohacking circles short peptides from this lineage are discussed as anti-ageing agents, and the appearance link is the broader hope that slower tissue ageing could show in skin and overall look; for Cortagen specifically, the published work concerns nerve, brain and heart tissue rather than skin or hair. Published studies are cell-culture, animal and small biochemical experiments, many from the developers' laboratory. They examined gene expression in mouse heart [1], interleukin-2 expression [2][4], sciatic nerve regeneration [5], free-radical processes [7] and chromatin condensation in old cells [8][9]. A Russian report compared Cortexin and Cortagen in rats with chronic cerebral ischaemia [10].
It is not an approved drug in Western countries and no published human trial in healthy people examines it for appearance.

sections.h: Origin: Khavinson and the peptide bioregulator idea
paras: Vladimir Khavinson (1946-2024) was a Russian gerontologist, director of the St. Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology and head of the gerontology chair at North-Western State Medical University; Wikipedia credits him with about 775 publications and 196 patents and records that he extracted peptide complexes from animal organs from 1973 and synthesised short peptides from them.[11] His group's concept is that short peptides act as signalling regulators of ageing processes and can be tailored to tissues, which is the framework in which Cortagen was designed.[1][11] The Wikipedia article on Khavinson notes that most cited evidence comes from his own institutes and carries a promotional-content flag, and that the same article describes six peptide medicines approved for use in the USSR and Russia.[11]

The 2004 mouse-heart study states that Cortagen was obtained by directed synthesis from amino-acid analysis of Cortexin and that, in humans, it had shown a pronounced effect on structural and functional recovery of peripheral nerve tissue after trauma, with other effects on cardiovascular and cerebrovascular parameters.[1]

A microarray study analysed 15,247 transcripts in the hearts of 6-month-old female CBA mice given Cortagen for five consecutive days and reported altered expression of a set of genes, which the authors framed as screening molecular targets of peptide bioregulators in ageing [1]. In rat and mouse cell systems, Cortagen had weaker immunomodulating effects than the related peptides Vilon and Epithalon: it produced no comitogenic effect on thymocytes [3] and a less pronounced effect on interleukin-2 mRNA in splenocytes [4], although in vivo work reported modulation of interleukin-2 expression in hypothalamic cells [2].

In rats whose sciatic nerve was cut and sutured, a ten-day course of Cortagen was reported to raise the growth rate of regenerating fibres by 27 percent and conduction velocity by 40 percent [5]. Epithalon and Cortagen reduced lipid-peroxidation products and protein oxidation in rat serum and cortex [7]. In ischaemic rats, Cortexin and Cortagen both sped recovery of disturbed behaviour and limited excessive lipid peroxidation [10].

Studies of old human lymphocytes in culture, from people aged 75 to 88, reported that short peptides including Cortagen decondensed tightly packed chromatin and activated ribosomal genes [8][9]. The authors interpret this as reversal of age-linked heterochromatinisation; these are laboratory findings in cells.

Nearly all of the published work comes from Khavinson's institute and collaborators, mostly in Russian-language or regional journals such as Bulletin of Experimental Biology and Medicine. Independent replication in Western laboratories is not part of the published record, and no controlled human trial of Cortagen has been published.

No studies found. The existing literature is limited to cell-culture, animal and chromatin work, plus one Russian-language report on brain ischaemia in rats [10]; the 2004 mouse-heart paper refers to human effects on nerve recovery but cites no trial in its abstract [1].

card.summary: Khavinson brain-derived tetrapeptide (AEDP) studied only in cells and animals; no appearance evidence.
card.note: Research is mostly from the developers' laboratory; not an appearance product.

quick.overview:
Cortagen is a four-amino-acid peptide (Ala-Glu-Asp-Pro) made by Vladimir Khavinson's Russian group, modelled on a brain-cortex peptide extract called Cortexin.

Studies are limited to cells, rodents and a few small reports. No human trial for appearance exists.
quick.mechanism: Its developers propose that short peptides regulate gene expression in a tissue-specific way. Studies report changes in gene and interleukin-2 expression in cell and animal models.
quick.risks: Human safety data are essentially absent from the published literature, and it is not an approved drug in Western countries.

chain: Short peptide proposed to regulate gene expression in specific tissues
Reported effects on nerve, brain and heart tissue in cell and animal work
Claimed slower tissue ageing; no appearance outcome studied
angle.text: Cortagen belongs to a family of Russian peptide bioregulators promoted for tissue-specific anti-ageing effects. Studies describe nerve repair, antioxidant and gene-expression changes in animals and cells; none measures skin, hair or facial ageing.
